title: Quality Studio core term catalogue
description: The shared semantic kernel every quality observation refers to. Aliases listed here are same-axis spelling variants that resolve without knowing the source contract; cross-contract projections of legacy vocabularies are adapters and live outside this catalogue.

axes.description: Who produced a record. Always explicit; absence never means agent.

terms.description: A language-model agent run produced the record.
A deterministic tool or analyzer produced the record.
A person authored the record.
The record was imported from an external system without a native producer.
The producer could not be established from evidence and was not assumed.

axes.description: How complete the evidence behind a record is. This describes coverage only; it is never a pass or a block.

terms.description: The evidence the profile expects was collected.
Some expected evidence was collected and some was not.
No expected evidence could be collected.

axes.description: What the evidence establishes for a review or one of its aspects.

terms.description: The evidence establishes conformance for the assessed scope.
The evidence establishes a weakness that does not by itself establish non-conformance.
The evidence establishes non-conformance for the assessed scope.
The scope was assessed but the evidence does not establish an outcome.
The scope does not apply to this subject.
The scope was not assessed by this producer.

axes.description: The direction of a before/after comparison. Used only for comparisons, never for a single-point assessment.

terms.description: The compared quality evidence is better after the change.
The compared quality evidence is worse after the change.
The comparison contains both improvement and regression.
The compared quality evidence is equivalent before and after the change.
The change did not touch anything the comparison observes.
A comparison was attempted but the evidence does not establish a direction.

axes.description: A policy disposition. It requires a policyRef and is never supplied by a raw finding or inferred from an assessment.

terms.description: The policy permits the subject to proceed.
The policy permits the subject to proceed and requires the warning to be surfaced.
The policy refuses the subject.
The policy declines to decide and names who or what decides next.

axes.description: How damaging one finding is. Ordering is meaningful; scoring weights stay in policy.

terms.description: Exploitable or breaking now, with no compensating control.
A defect with a direct and likely path to damage.
A defect that needs a further condition to cause damage.
A defect with limited reach or an available compensating control.
An observation recorded without a damage claim.

axes.description: The human disposition of a cross-observation issue. It lives in lifecycle events, never in an observation.

terms.description: The issue is unresolved and not dispositioned.
The issue is real and its risk was explicitly accepted.
The issue is out of scope for this subject by explicit decision.
The issue was judged not to exist in the assessed subject.
The issue was fixed and the fix is backed by a resolution basis.

axes.description: What kind of artefact one evidence item points at.

terms.description: A location in reviewed source.
The outcome of an executed test.
A measured runtime value.
Structured output of a deterministic tool.
A stored build or run artefact.
A specification, standard, or other prose source.
A person's recorded statement.

objects.description: One producer's immutable result for one exact subject and input set.
One aspect judgement inside an observation.
One evidenced defect inside an observation.
The identity block of whoever produced the record.
One typed reference to the material a judgement rests on.
A versioned policy's disposition over an observation.
A before/after comparison of two subjects.
One append-only disposition event for a cross-observation issue.

aspects.description: Whether the code does what it is specified to do.
Whether the structure of the unit matches the intended architecture.
Security weaknesses that no more specific security aspect covers.
Credentials or other secret material exposed in the subject.
Whether callers are identified and their actions authorized.
Whether untrusted input is validated before it is trusted.
Security of configuration and infrastructure definitions.
What the subject exposes across a trust boundary.
Business rules that a caller can bypass or abuse without breaking a technical control.
Whether catalogued attacks against a boundary were assessed.
Runtime cost and responsiveness of the subject.
Risk the change introduces relative to its stated intent.
Whether the change is backed by test evidence.
Whether the change stays inside its stated scope.
Whether the change moves the codebase away from the intended architecture.
